<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</span></span></span></span></div>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text">Narrow bit-width data formats are key to reducing the computational and storage costs of modern deep learning applications. This paper evaluates Microscaling (MX) data formats that combine a per-block scaling factor with narrow floating-point and integer types for individual elements.
MX formats balance the competing needs of hardware efficiency, model accuracy, and user friction.
Empirical results on over two dozen benchmarks demonstrate practicality of MX data formats as a drop-in replacement for baseline FP32 for AI inference and training with low user friction. We also show the first instance of training generative language models at sub-8-bit weights, activations, <span id="abstract1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">and</span> gradients with minimal accuracy loss and no modifications to the training recipe.</span></p>
  
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Recent advances in AI capabilities such as conversational question answering,
intelligent code completion, and text-to-image generation have seen rapid adoption in practical technologies.
These advances have been realized primarily through scaling up the size of the underlying deep learning model.
However, this scaling up has led to a significant increase in the computing power and storage capacity necessary to train and deploy such models.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">One method to reduce deep learning models’ computational and storage cost is to use low bit-width data formats instead of the conventional FP32.
Great strides have been made to enable training using FP16, Bfloat16, and most recently FP8 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>, as well as to perform inference in narrow integer formats like INT8.
Native support for low bit-width formats is now commonplace in AI-oriented hardware such as GPUs, TPUs, and edge inference devices.
The narrowest formats, such as FP8 and INT8, require per-tensor scaling factors to adjust to the dynamic range of each tensor. Tensor level scaling has has been shown to be insufficient, though, for sub-8-bit formats due to their limited dynamic range.
Research has shown that micro scaled data formats that associate scaling factors with fine-grained sub-blocks of a tensor are more effective in sub-8 bit regime (e.g., <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">2</a>; <a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">3</a>; <a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">4</a>; <a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">5</a>]</cite>).</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">This paper evaluates Microscaling (MX) data formats <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite> — the first open standard for a family of micro-scaled datatypes aimed at deep learning training and inference. The MX standard aims to create an effective data format by achieving a balance among three key factors:</p>
<ul id="S1.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S1.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hardware Efficiency</span> — Maximize compute and storage efficiency via reduced bit-width.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Model Accuracy</span> — Minimize the gap in the quality of results compared with baseline FP32 for AI training and inference.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S1.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S1.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S1.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">User Friction</span> — Ensure seamless integration within existing training and inference frameworks and generalizability across different workloads.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S1.p3.2" class="ltx_p">Details on the MX standard and the concrete binary formats can be found in the OCP Microscaling Specification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>. This paper will focus on the empirical results of using MX formats for direct-cast inference, error diffusion inference, and finetuned inference, as well as training on various benchmarks.
Our results corroborate the effectiveness of MX formats in balancing the competing demands of hardware efficiency, model accuracy, and user friction.
8-bit MX formats can perform inference directly on FP32 pretrained models with minimal accuracy loss and without the need for calibration or finetuning.
Inference with 6-bit MX formats is also very close to FP32 after quantization-aware fine-tuning or using a post-training quantization method.
Using 6-bit MX formats, we demonstrate the first instance of training large transformer models with sub-8-bit weights, activations, and gradients to an accuracy matching FP32 without modifications to the training recipe.
Going even further, we show that training of large transformers can be done with 4-bit MX format weights, incurring only a minor accuracy drop.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">The custom CUDA library to emulate MX formats on existing GPUs can be found at <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">7</a>]</cite>. This library can be used to reproduce the experimental results reported in this paper.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span>Microscaling</h2>

<div id="S2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">A basic unit of data in an MX format represents a vector of <math id="S2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> numbers and consists of a single <span id="S2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">shared scale</span> <math id="S2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> and <math id="S2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> scalar <span id="S2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">elements</span> <math id="S2.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{P_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">{</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{P_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}</annotation></semantics></math> (see Figure <a href="#S2.F1" title="Figure 1 ‣ 2 Microscaling ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>). This unit of data is called an MX block and is defined by the combination of <span id="S2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">block size</span> <math id="S2.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math>, scale data format, and element data format. The two data formats are independent of one another, and all <math id="S2.p1.m6" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> elements share the same element data format.
The layout of an MX block is not prescribed — an implementation may store <math id="S2.p1.m7" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> contiguously with or separately from the elements.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.F1" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S2.F1.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S2.F1.2.1" class="ltx_text"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2310.10537v3/MXFP_OCP_fig1.svg" id="S2.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:333/141;" width="333" height="141"></object></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span>A single block in a Microscaling data format.
The block encodes a vector of <math id="S2.F1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> numbers, each with value <math id="S2.F1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="XP_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">XP_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Let <math id="S2.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">{</mo><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{v_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}</annotation></semantics></math> be the <math id="S2.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> real numbers represented in an MX block. The value of each number can be inferred as follows:</p>
<ul id="S2.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S2.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X=\text{NaN}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo>=</mo><mtext>NaN</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X=\text{NaN}</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}=\text{NaN}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mtext>NaN</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}=\text{NaN}</annotation></semantics></math> for all <math id="S2.I1.i1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>i</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">If <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="|XP_{i}|&gt;Vmax_{Float32}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo>&gt;</mo><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|XP_{i}|&gt;Vmax_{Float32}</annotation></semantics></math> then <math id="S2.I1.i2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is implementation-defined</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S2.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;padding-top:0.0pt;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S2.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Otherwise, <math id="S2.I1.i3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="v_{i}=XP_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>v</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">v_{i}=XP_{i}</annotation></semantics></math></p>
</div></li>
</ul>
<p id="S2.p2.2" class="ltx_p">where <math id="S2.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="Vmax_{Float32}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>V</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>F</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mn>32</mn></mrow></msub></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">Vmax_{Float32}</annotation></semantics></math> refers to the largest representable magnitude in IEEE Float32.</p>
</div>
<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>Special Value Encodings</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">MX formats can encode NaN in up to two ways. First: if <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> is NaN, then all <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> values in the MX block is NaN regardless of the encodings of <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{i}</annotation></semantics></math>. Second: if <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> is not NaN, each element <math id="S2.SS1.p1.m5" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> may individually encode NaN.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Depending on the element format, MX formats can encode Inf by letting <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> be a number (i.e., not a NaN) and each <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> individually encode Inf. The shared scale <math id="S2.SS1.p2.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>X</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X</annotation></semantics></math> does not encode Inf.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>Concrete MX Formats</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S2.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ 2.2 Concrete MX Formats ‣ 2 Microscaling ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> shows the parameters that define the concrete MX formats, which are named by prepending "MX" to the name of the element data format. All concrete MX formats use E8M0 (an 8-bit exponent) as the format for the shared scale. The representable exponents of these formats is a superset of the representable exponents of FP32.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Details on the FP8 element data formats can be found in the OCP FP8 specification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">1</a>]</cite>. Details on the other element data formats and the E8M0 scale format can be found in the OCP Microscaling Specification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S2.T1" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Concrete MX-compliant data formats and their parameters.</figcaption>
<table id="S2.T1.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_guessed_headers ltx_align_middle">
<thead class="ltx_thead">
<tr id="S2.T1.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S2.T1.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Format</span></th>
<th id="S2.T1.2.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T1.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Block</span></th>
<th id="S2.T1.2.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T1.2.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scale</span></th>
<th id="S2.T1.2.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T1.2.1.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scale</span></th>
<th id="S2.T1.2.1.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T1.2.1.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Element</span></th>
<th id="S2.T1.2.1.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r ltx_border_t"><span id="S2.T1.2.1.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Element</span></th></tr>
<tr id="S2.T1.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<th id="S2.T1.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_l ltx_border_r"><span id="S2.T1.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Name</span></th>
<th id="S2.T1.2.2.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r"><span id="S2.T1.2.2.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Size</span></th>
<th id="S2.T1.2.2.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r"><span id="S2.T1.2.2.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Data Format</span></th>
<th id="S2.T1.2.2.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r"><span id="S2.T1.2.2.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bits</span></th>
<th id="S2.T1.2.2.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r"><span id="S2.T1.2.2.5.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Data Format</span></th>
<th id="S2.T1.2.2.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_th ltx_th_column ltx_border_r"><span id="S2.T1.2.2.6.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Bit-width</span></th></tr>
</thead>
<tbody class="ltx_tbody">
<tr id="S2.T1.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S2.T1.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt">MXFP8</td>
<td id="S2.T1.2.3.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt">32</td>
<td id="S2.T1.2.3.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt">E8M0</td>
<td id="S2.T1.2.3.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt">8</td>
<td id="S2.T1.2.3.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt">FP8 (E4M3 / E5M2)</td>

</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span>Scalar Float to MX Format Conversion</h2>

<div id="S3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this paper, we use Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 3 Scalar Float to MX Format Conversion ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a> for conversion from scalar floating-point format (e.g., FP32) to an MX format. This algorithm follows the semantics outlined in Section 6.3 of the OCP Microscaling Specification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>, and is provided as a working example. Note that, the specification allows for other implementation-defined conversion recipes — i.e., conversion to MX formats is <span id="S3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">not necessarily required</span> to follow Algorithm <math id="S3.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>1</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">1</annotation></semantics></math>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="alg1" class="ltx_float ltx_float_algorithm ltx_framed ltx_framed_top">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_float"><span id="alg1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Algorithm 1</span> </span> Convert vector of scalar floats <math id="alg1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">{</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{V_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}</annotation></semantics></math> to an MX block
<math id="alg1.m4" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\{X,\&gt;\{P_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">{</mo><mi>X</mi><mo rspace="0.367em">,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">{</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">}</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\{X,\&gt;\{P_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}\}</annotation></semantics></math></figcaption>

<div id="alg1.l0" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l0.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">0:</span></span>
            
            
           <math id="alg1.l0.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="emax_{elem}=\text{exponent of the largest normal number in the element data format}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mrow><mo>=</mo><mtext>exponent of the largest normal number in the element data format</mtext></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">emax_{elem}=\text{exponent of the largest normal number in the element data format}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l1" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l1.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">1:</span></span>
            
            
           <math id="alg1.l1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="shared\_exp\leftarrow\lfloor\log_{2}(\max_{i}(|V_{i}|))\rfloor-emax_{elem}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><mrow><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">⌊</mo><mrow><msub><mi>log</mi><mn>2</mn></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>max</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>⁡</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo stretchy="false">|</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em" stretchy="true">⌋</mo></mrow><mo>−</mo><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><msub><mi>x</mi><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow></msub></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">shared\_exp\leftarrow\lfloor\log_{2}(\max_{i}(|V_{i}|))\rfloor-emax_{elem}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l2" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l2.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">2:</span></span>
            
            
           <math id="alg1.l2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X\leftarrow 2^{shared\_exp}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo stretchy="false">←</mo><msup><mn>2</mn><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X\leftarrow 2^{shared\_exp}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
<div id="alg1.l3" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l3.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">3:</span></span>
            
            
           <span id="alg1.l3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span> <math id="alg1.l3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="i=1" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">i=1</annotation></semantics></math> to <math id="alg1.l3.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> <span id="alg1.l3.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">do</span>



</div>
<div id="alg1.l4" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l4.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">4:</span></span>
            
            
            <math id="alg1.l4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{i}=quantize\_to\_element\_format(V_{i}/X)" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>=</mo><mrow><mi>q</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>u</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>i</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>z</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>n</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>o</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>t</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{i}=quantize\_to\_element\_format(V_{i}/X)</annotation></semantics></math>, clamping normal numbers

</div>
<div id="alg1.l5" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l5.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">5:</span></span>
            
            
           <span id="alg1.l5.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">end</span> <span id="alg1.l5.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">for</span>
</div>
<div id="alg1.l6" class="ltx_listingline">
            <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_listingline"><span id="alg1.l6.1" class="ltx_text" style="font-size:80%;">6:</span></span>
            
            
           <span id="alg1.l6.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">return</span>  <math id="alg1.l6.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="X,\&gt;\{P_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>X</mi><mo rspace="0.367em">,</mo><msubsup><mrow><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">{</mo><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo maxsize="0.900em" minsize="0.900em">}</mo></mrow><mrow><mi>i</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><mi>k</mi></msubsup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">X,\&gt;\{P_{i}\}_{i=1}^{k}</annotation></semantics></math>

</div>
</div>
</figure>
<div id="S3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">On Line 1, <math id="S3.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="shared\_exp" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>s</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>h</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>r</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>d</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>p</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">shared\_exp</annotation></semantics></math> contains an offset of <math id="S3.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="emax\_elem" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>a</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>x</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>_</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>l</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>e</mi><mo lspace="0em" rspace="0em">​</mo><mi>m</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">emax\_elem</annotation></semantics></math> to map the max input exponent to the largest binade in the element data format. This enables full utilization of the element data format’s exponent range.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">On Line 4, when quantizing <math id="S3.p3.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{i}/X" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mrow><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><mo>/</mo><mi>X</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{i}/X</annotation></semantics></math>, normal numbers that exceed the representable range of the element format are clamped to the maximum representable value, preserving the sign. Infs and NaNs are not clamped. This is in accordance with the OCP MX specification.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">On Line 4, <math id="S3.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="P_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>P</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">P_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is set to zero if the corresponding input <math id="S3.p4.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="V_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>V</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">V_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> is a subnormal Float32 number. This is not described in the OCP MX specification and was done to simplify the algorithm.</p>
</div>
<div id="S3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">When converting multi-dimensional tensors, a principle axis must be selected for the shared scale (typically the reduction dimension in matrix multiplication). For a 2D matrix, the scale can be shared by every <math id="S3.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="k" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mi>k</mi><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">k</annotation></semantics></math> element in a row or column. Transposing a 2D matrix in an MX format changes the axis of the shared scale — i.e., conversion to MX format and transposing are not commutative operations.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experimental Results</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Compute Flow</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.1 Compute Flow ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> shows an example compute flow for training using an MX format.
For operations involving dot products (e.g., matmul and convolution) in both forward and backward passes, the two inputs are converted to MX format, and the operation is performed using the efficient dot product from Section 6.2 of the OCP Microscaling Specification <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">6</a>]</cite>.
Vector operations (e.g., layernorm, Softmax, GELU, and residual add) are performed in a scalar floating-point format like Bfloat16 or FP32.
The dot product operations produce outputs in the scalar float format.
A master copy of the weights is kept in FP32, and this copy is updated in each training step. In all the training examples in this paper, we use the compute flow illustrated in Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.1 Compute Flow ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F2" class="ltx_figure">
<p id="S4.F2.2" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center"><span id="S4.F2.2.1" class="ltx_text"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2310.10537v3/MX_compute_flow.svg" id="S4.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/227;" width="476" height="227"></object></span></p>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>Compute flow with MX formats (denoted as MX*). In the diagram, MatMul includes any dot product operation such as matmul, linear, and convolution. Vector Ops include non-dot product operations like activations, normalization, Softmax, and residual add.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">Due to non-commutative nature of transpose and quantization into MX formats (see Section <a href="#S3" title="3 Scalar Float to MX Format Conversion ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), the quantized weights <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{i}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{i}</annotation></semantics></math> and their transpose <math id="S4.SS1.p2.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="W_{i}^{T}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msubsup><mi>W</mi><mi>i</mi><mi>T</mi></msubsup><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">W_{i}^{T}</annotation></semantics></math> must be stored as two separate tensors.
Note that the two tensors do not need to be stored in working memory simultaneously unless a very fine-grained interleaving of the forward and backward passes is employed.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Methodology</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We used a custom library to emulate MX formats on existing GPUs. The library is implemented as a custom CUDA extension in PyTorch and performs quantization following Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.1 Compute Flow ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. In particular, we explored four settings:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<ul id="S4.I1" class="ltx_itemize">
<li id="S4.I1.i1" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Direct-cast Inference</span>. The quantized inference is performed on a trained FP32 model. All GeMMs in the forward pass are quantized unless explicitly called out otherwise (the backward pass is not executed at all).</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i2" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Error Diffusion Inference</span>. The error diffusion algorithm is a Post Training Quantization (PTQ) algorithm derived from GPFQ  <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">8</a>]</cite>. It performs quantization using a small calibration dataset. In this experiment, all activations and weights in the forward pass are quantized to the same format for simplicity. This PTQ process is a quick one-pass process without a training loop or needing any tuning parameter.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i3" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Finetuned Inference</span>. Quantization-aware finetuning is done on a trained FP32 model for a small number of epochs. For this fine-tuning, all GeMMs in the forward pass are quantized, while the backward pass is performed in FP32. Hyperparameter exploration is used to find proper finetuning hyperparameters.</p>
</div></li>
<li id="S4.I1.i4" class="ltx_item" style="list-style-type:none;"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_item">•</span> 
<div id="S4.I1.i4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.I1.i4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Training</span>. A model is trained from scratch using a compute flow where all GeMMs in both forward and backward passes are quantized (see Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.1 Compute Flow ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>. For mixed-precision training where the weights and activations use different data formats, the gradients (<math id="S4.I1.i4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\text{E}_{\text{i}}" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><msub><mtext>E</mtext><mtext>i</mtext></msub><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\text{E}_{\text{i}}</annotation></semantics></math> in Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.1 Compute Flow ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) are quantized to the activation format.</p>
</div></li>
</ul>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Our benchmark suite contains two types of tasks: discriminative and generative.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>Discriminative Inference</h3>

<div id="S4.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In this section, we examine inference results with MX formats across a variety of discriminative tasks including language translation, text encoding, image classification, speech recognition, and recommendation models. Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Discriminative Inference ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> summarizes the results related to <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">direct-cast inference</span>. Results for <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">finetuned inference</span> are reported in Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Discriminative Inference ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, and results for <span id="S4.SS3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">PTQ with error diffusion inference</span> are reported in Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.3 Discriminative Inference ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In these experiments, the same MX formats were used for both weights and activations following Algorithm <a href="#alg1" title="Algorithm 1 ‣ 3 Scalar Float to MX Format Conversion ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>. Round-half-to-nearest-even was used for conversion to MX formats. The results presented in Table <a href="#S4.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Discriminative Inference ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a> corroborates the effectiveness of MXINT8 as a drop-in replacement for FP32 with minimal accuracy drop.
For MXFP8 and MXFP6, the general trend is that the variant of the format with more mantissa bits was better for direct-cast inference.
With finetuned inference (Table <a href="#S4.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ 4.3 Discriminative Inference ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>), MXFP6_E2M3 is able to achieve close-to-parity with FP32.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T2" class="ltx_table">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Direct-cast inference with MX data formats. For each experiment, the FP32 baseline was quantized (both weights and activations) with no additional tweaks. MXINT8 is a compelling alternative to FP32 for low-friction direct-cast inference.

<section id="S4.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.4 </span>Generative Inference</h3>

<div id="S4.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We leveraged the open source LM Eval Harness by Eleuther AI for our evaluation of MX data formats in generative inference of OpenAI GPT3-175B and open source LLaMA-7B.<span id="footnote1" class="ltx_note ltx_role_footnote"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup><span class="ltx_note_outer"><span class="ltx_note_content"><sup class="ltx_note_mark">1</sup>
              <span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_note">1</span>
              
              
              
            https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness/tree/1736d78dd9615107e68ec7f74043b02d4ab68d12.</span></span></span> All benchmarks were run under zero-shot settings (i.e., no examples were presented to the models before evaluation). Our benchmark suite includes the following subset:</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Lambada</span> — Lambada is a long range prediction task, where the model must predict the last word in a long narrative passage. We used the version of lambada data used to evaluate GPT2 in LM Harness.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Wikitext</span> — The wikitext task is based on the wikitext-2 dataset and requires the model to predict long sequences based on high quality Wikipedia articles.
GPT3-175B was not evaluated on this task as Wikipedia data was part of its training corpus <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p4.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ARC dataset</span> — The Arc tasks are both multiple choice tasks consisting of nearly <math id="S4.SS4.p4.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="8000" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>8000</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">8000</annotation></semantics></math> science exam questions, with the dataset split into easy and more challenging questions. The model is tasked with picking the correct answer from several options.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p5.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S4.SS4.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hendryck’s Test</span> — Hendryck’s test suite is a set of tasks that measure how knowledgeable a model is in <math id="S4.SS4.p5.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="57" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mn>57</mn><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">57</annotation></semantics></math> different fields. We used <span id="S4.SS4.p5.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">computer science</span>, <span id="S4.SS4.p5.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">international law</span>, and <span id="S4.SS4.p5.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">jurisprudence</span> as a subset for this study. These tasks are all multiple choice questions, where the model must pick the correct answer from the options presented.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p6.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ 4.4 Generative Inference ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a> and Table <a href="#S4.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ 4.4 Generative Inference ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a> show results for direct-cast inference on OpenAI GPT3-175B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">17</a>]</cite> and open source LLaMA-7B, respectively.
Due to the size of these models, no quantization-aware finetuning was performed. The columns with a single MX format use that format for both weights and activations; the other columns list separate formats for weights (Wt) and activations (Act) and utilize mixed-precision.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS4.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS4.p7.1" class="ltx_p">MXINT8 matched baseline FP32 to within the standard deviation on all tasks for both GPT3-175B and LLaMA-7B. MXINT8 once again proves to be a compelling alternative to FP32 for low-friction direct-cast inference.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.T5" class="ltx_table">

<section id="S4.SS5" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.5 </span>Generative Training</h3>

<div id="S4.SS5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 4.5 Generative Training ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> and Figure  <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Table 7 ‣ 4.5 Generative Training ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> show the language model loss obtained from training GPT-like models of various size (20M-1.5B) using MXFP6_e3m2 for both the forward and backward passes (see Figure <a href="#S4.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 4.1 Compute Flow ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>).
The training is done using the ADAM optimizer, with hyperparameters tuned for FP32. The same hyperparameters were reused for the MX format runs with no changes. All the models are trained to efficiency with number of steps calculated based on the scaling power-laws <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite">[<a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">18</a>]</cite>. Round-half-away-from-zero rounding was used for conversion to MX formats.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">The results in Table <a href="#S4.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ 4.5 Generative Training ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a> and Figure  <a href="#S4.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Table 7 ‣ 4.5 Generative Training ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a> show that MXFP6_e3m2 is capable of delivering a model quality matching that of FP32 at much lower circuitry footprint.
<span id="S4.SS5.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">MXFP6 provides the first demonstration of training generative language models to parity with FP32 using 6-bit weights, activations, and gradients with no modification to the training recipe.</span></p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Pushing the limits even further, Table <a href="#S4.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ 4.5 Generative Training ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a> and Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ Table 8 ‣ 4.5 Generative Training ‣ 4 Experimental Results ‣ Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a> show the results from training the same GPT-like models, this time under a mixed-precision setting with MXFP4 weights and MXFP6_e3m2 activations. The gradients used the same data format as the activations.
The training hyperparameters were the same as before.
<span id="S4.SS5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Our results demonstrate that generative language models can be trained with MXFP4 weights and MXFP6 activations and gradients incurring only a minor penalty in the model loss.</span> This is once again with no modifications to the training recipe.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>GPT mixed-precision training loss curve, using MXFP4 for weights and MXFP6_E3M2 for activations and gradients.</figcaption>

</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Conclusion</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">This paper evaluates MX data formats that integrate a block-level scale on top of narrow bit-width elements.
The evaluated concrete MX formats provide compelling alternatives to FP32 training and inference with minimal user friction.
Experimental results show the effectiveness of MX formats for a variety of deep learning models including generative language models, image classification, speech recognition, recommendation models, and translation.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">In particular, MXINT8 is a compelling drop-in replacement to FP32 for low-friction direct-cast inference.
MXFP6 closely matches FP32 for inference after quantization-aware finetuning.
MXFP6 also, for the first time, enables generative language model training at sub-8-bit weights, activations, and gradients without sacrificing model accuracy or needing changes to the training recipe.
Reducing the bit-width even further, we showcase training with MXFP4 weights and MXFP6 activations and gradients, incurring only a minor loss penalty for generative language models.</p>
</div>
</section>

    <p>We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile
      support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the
      methods listed below:</p>
    <ul>
      <li>Click the "Report Issue" <span class="mobile-only">(<svg role="presentation"
            style="display: inline-block; vertical-align: middle; fill: var(--text-color);" aria-hidden="true"

              d="M224 160C224 107 267 64 320 64C373 64 416 107 416 160L416 163.6C416 179.3 403.3 192 387.6 192L252.5 192C236.8 192 224.1 179.3 224.1 163.6L224.1 160zM569.6 172.8C580.2 186.9 577.3 207 563.2 217.6L465.4 290.9C470.7 299.8 474.7 309.6 477.2 320L576 320C593.7 320 608 334.3 608 352C608 369.7 593.7 384 576 384L480 384L480 416C480 418.6 479.9 421.3 479.8 423.9L563.2 486.4C577.3 497 580.2 517.1 569.6 531.2C559 545.3 538.9 548.2 524.8 537.6L461.7 490.3C438.5 534.5 395.2 566.5 344 574.2L344 344C344 330.7 333.3 320 320 320C306.7 320 296 330.7 296 344L296 574.2C244.8 566.5 201.5 534.5 178.3 490.3L115.2 537.6C101.1 548.2 81 545.3 70.4 531.2C59.8 517.1 62.7 497 76.8 486.4L160.2 423.9C160.1 421.3 160 418.7 160 416L160 384L64 384C46.3 384 32 369.7 32 352C32 334.3 46.3 320 64 320L162.8 320C165.3 309.6 169.3 299.8 174.6 290.9L76.8 217.6C62.7 207 59.8 186.9 70.4 172.8C81 158.7 101.1 155.8 115.2 166.4L224 248C236.3 242.9 249.8 240 264 240L376 240C390.2 240 403.7 242.8 416 248L524.8 166.4C538.9 155.8 559 158.7 569.6 172.8z" />
          </svg>)</span> button, located in the page header.</li>

    <p><strong>Tip:</strong> You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.</p>
    <p>Our team has already identified <a class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/arXiv/html_feedback/issues"
        target="_blank">the following issues</a>. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we
      may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability
      should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for
      all.</p>
    <p>Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a <a
        class="ltx_ref" href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/wiki/Porting-LaTeX-packages-for-LaTeXML"
        target="_blank">list of packages that need conversion</a>, and welcome <a class="ltx_ref"
        href="https://github.com/brucemiller/LaTeXML/issues" target="_blank">developer contributions</a>.</p>
